name: Brian Schottenheimer

views.text: Players play harder for coaches who show them they care, so the relationship comes before the scheme.
A good quarterback's leadership is worth as much as his arm, and he says so loudly when he sees it.
A bad loss is a time to keep the room together and lean on the people in it, not to change who you are.
Rookies and undrafted players should feel the coaches know their names and want them there from day one.
Sitting in the other side of the ball's meetings makes an offensive coach better at his own job.
A coach who changes his personality when he gets a bigger title usually fails; stay the same man.
A losing season starts with the head coach; own it first, then dig out what went wrong.
Fights in practice cost the whole team, so the whole team pays for them.
Players tune out repetition, so the meetings and the message should change every year.

signatures: praises his quarterback in sweeping terms, often reaching for a comparison to an all-time great
shows emotion openly on the sideline and in team meetings, and talks about it afterward
talks about friendships with other coaches and what he learned from them
repeats his praise for a new assistant's communication several times in the same answer

motivation.want: to prove a career assistant can lead a team deep into January
motivation.fear: that his first head coaching job ends before his culture work pays off

want.text: a high-scoring offense paired with a rebuilt Dallas defense

fear.text: a second straight year out of the playoffs

voice: Loud, warm and emotional; he speaks quickly with visible enthusiasm and hands out praise by name, especially to quarterbacks and new assistants. He owns losses in the first person and promises to get to the bottom of them, and his temper shows when players fight in practice. He keeps criticism of individual players inside the building.

evidence.summary: Hiring story when Dallas made him head coach: son of Marty Schottenheimer, coaching since 1997 with the Rams, Jets, Seahawks and Colts among others, a Cowboys consultant in 2022 and coordinator in 2023-24 while McCarthy called plays. Prescott had his best season in 2023 when the offense led the league in scoring; it fell to 21st in 2024 after Prescott's injury. Facts, little on personality.

Rookie minicamp piece in his first months as head coach: he moves among draft picks and undrafted players starting conversations, players call him energetic and fun but serious when needed, and he wants players to feel cared for and close to their assistants. He adds music to practice, reshuffles meeting and locker room seats, and plans to work closely with the quarterbacks. Describes himself as demanding and says coaches who change their personality fail.

Feature on his friendship with Dan Quinn, dating to the 2007-08 Jets staff. McCarthy brought him to Dallas as a consultant in 2022 when he meant to take a year off, and he sat in Quinn's defensive meetings playing the opposing offense; the two stayed late talking leadership and culture. He calls Quinn a close friend, admits he had lost some passion for coaching before regaining it, and comes across as reflective and family-minded.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Cowboys on SI), Randy Gurzi
evidence.summary: Prescott says his head coach is openly emotional and that players feed off it and play harder for him. The piece credits him with steadying the team after a 3-5-1 start and the death of Marshawn Kneeland, before three straight wins. Fan-network framing around a player quote.

In his first camp as head coach, after several practice fights, he makes the whole team and some coaches run, sends a rookie lineman off for throwing a punch, and shouts a profane challenge at the fighters; CeeDee Lamb publicly backs the discipline. One episode.

After a 7-9-1 first season ends with a loss to the Giants, he says he expected the playoffs and a Super Bowl push, takes responsibility for falling short, and promises to find out what went wrong. Short report on his postgame remarks.

At his new coordinator's introduction he calls Christian Parker wise beyond his years and convicted in his beliefs, notes he himself became a coordinator at 32, says Parker has prepared for the job for years, and says Dallas hit a home run with the hire after nine coordinator interviews.

State of the Cowboys address opening camp: he calls missing the playoffs unacceptable, repeatedly praises Parker as a communicator whose office players keep visiting, says he changed how the team grades film and runs meetings, and wants to avoid routine because players tune out repetition.
